summary: A reply defending the Telnet Go-Ahead mechanism against objections in RFC 596. The author argues that disliking line-at-a-time systems is a matter of taste and that Go-Ahead will work well between reasonably implemented hosts.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 595 defends the Telnet Go Ahead signal, especially for systems that process input one line at a time. The author says it can mark the end of server output and argues that servers should still implement it.

questions: what did rfc 595 say go ahead does
subtitle: An argument for keeping Telnet Go Ahead useful to line-at-a-time systems.

tldr.problem: The author responds to objections to Telnet Go Ahead and explains why it can help line-at-a-time systems and their users.
tldr.mechanism: Go Ahead can signal that a server has finished sending output, letting a user Telnet handle a complete response rather than treating every character as a separate end point.
tldr.outcome: The author opposes removing the requirement for servers to implement Go Ahead and argues that suppressing it when appropriate has little cost.

today: RFC 595 is a 1973 discussion defending the Telnet Go Ahead mechanism and setting out its author's position in a protocol debate.

sections.title: Why Line-at-a-Time Systems Need a Signal
sections.content:
Line-at-a-time systems buffer typed characters until an end-of-line signal arrives, so the system does not recognize a partially entered line. The author argues that this operating mode, rather than the terminal itself, determines whether Go Ahead is useful.

In a server-to-user exchange, Go Ahead can assure the receiving system that the server has finished sending output for now. The author says this can help a user Telnet avoid handling each arriving character separately.
sections.plainLanguage: A line-at-a-time system holds typed characters until it receives a complete line. Go Ahead can tell it that the server has finished its current output, so it can turn control back to the user.

sections.title: When the Server Sends Go Ahead
sections.content:
The author says a server should send Go Ahead when it has reasonable assurance that it will not produce more output, such as after a prompt. If more output does follow, the server can send it and then send another Go Ahead. A multi-line output, such as an editor printout, would have one Go Ahead at the end.

For links between users on different kinds of systems, the author also describes manually sending Go Ahead as a workable practice, while noting that mixed system output and user input needs more definition.
sections.plainLanguage: A server can send Go Ahead when it expects to pause, often after a prompt. If more output comes later, it can send that output followed by another signal.

sections.title: The Author's Position on the Proposal
sections.content:
The author accepts that making Suppress Go Ahead the default could be acceptable. However, he says the proposal he is answering would remove the requirement for all servers to implement Go Ahead, which he opposes because line-at-a-time users benefit from it.

The RFC also discusses the transition schedule and argues for implementations that accept either Telnet mode rather than relying on a second socket. These are the author's views in this reply, not a report that the proposed changes were adopted.
sections.plainLanguage: The author would accept suppressing Go Ahead by default, but not eliminating the requirement to implement it. He argues that line-at-a-time users need the option.
